36.title: Water to the west
36.hook: at Hardwar, seeing pilgrims throw water toward the rising sun, he throws his westward, to water his fields
36.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the Hardwar sakhi as a teaching that outward ritual without inner meaning does not reach God; a gurdwara at Hardwar marks the place tradition links to the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sajjan's rest house, and a robber who heard himself in a hymn. Your line was even Sajjan turned. Did you catch yourself writing someone off? Day thirty-six.

The old joke goes like this. A woman always cut the end off the roast before she cooked it. Her daughter asked why. Because my mother did. So they asked the grandmother, who said: my pan was too small. A habit can outlive its reason. Today's story happens on a riverbank at dawn. Hardwar, a pilgrimage town where the Ganges comes down out of the mountains. Crowds are standing in the cold river at sunrise. And a stranger from the Punjab wades in among them and does something that makes everyone stop and stare.
screen: `THE ROAST, AND THE SMALL PAN.` → `HARDWAR, ON THE GANGES, AT DAWN.` → `A STRANGER WADES IN.`

segments.voice: The pilgrims were cupping water in their hands and throwing it toward the rising sun, in the east. Tradition says it was an offering, meant to reach their ancestors in the next world. Nanak turned his back to the sun and began throwing water the other way, west. People gathered. What are you doing? He answered, as the story goes, that he was watering his fields back home in the Punjab. They laughed. Your fields are far away, in the Punjab. How can water thrown here reach them? And there's the turn. If your water can reach your ancestors in another world, he asked, why can't mine reach my fields in the Punjab? It's a funny story, and it's meant to be. But notice what Nanak is doing, and what he's not doing. He isn't mocking the pilgrims' love for their parents and grandparents. He's asking them to look at the act. Why do we do this? Does the water go where we think it goes? What would actually help? That question runs right through his hymns. Again and again, he says that washing the body at holy places doesn't wash the mind, and that what God looks at is the heart and the way a person lives. It's worth saying carefully: for the Hindus at Hardwar, then and now, bathing in the Ganges carries deep meaning, and this story is told by Sikhs about their Guru. It's his question, not a verdict on anyone's grandmother. And the question travels. Any family, any office can have water it throws east without asking why.
screen: `PILGRIMS THROWING WATER EAST.` · `NANAK THROWS IT WEST.` · `IF YOURS REACHES THEM, WHY NOT MINE?` · `LOOK AT THE ACT, NOT JUST THE HABIT.` · then, large: `WHY DO WE DO THIS?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: question one habit, gently. Settle, and breathe. Pick something you do every day without thinking. The route you drive. The way you start a meeting. Something you always say. Ask it, kindly, the way you'd ask a child: why do we do this? Maybe there's a great reason, and you'll keep it gladly. Maybe the pan was just too small. Either way, you'll know. The bell holds the time.
Water to the west. Guru Nanak at Hardwar, throwing water toward his own fields, to ask what an act really does. Today's word.
Your line: why do we do this. Today, ask it once out loud, about something at work or at home, and listen to the answer. Day thirty-six.

37.title: Feet toward the Kaaba
37.hook: tradition says that at Mecca, told his feet pointed at God's house, he asked them to turn his feet where God is not
37.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the Mecca sakhi, recorded by Bhai Gurdas in his first Var, as a teaching that God is present in every direction; it is often told alongside the Hardwar story as a pair.

segments.voice: Yesterday, water to the west at Hardwar. Your line was why do we do this. Which habit did you ask, and did it have a good answer? Day thirty-seven.

Yesterday Nanak stood in the Ganges. Today, tradition takes him about as far west as his journeys go: to Mecca, where the Kaaba stands, the house Muslims face when they pray, from every corner of the earth. Picture a long day of travel. A tired man in a traveler's clothes lies down to sleep, and without thinking about it, stretches out with his feet pointing toward the Kaaba. In the morning a qazi, a religious judge, finds him there. And he's upset, for a reason anyone can understand: to point your feet at something is, in that culture as in his own, a sign of disrespect. Today, what Nanak said back.
screen: `AS FAR WEST AS THE JOURNEYS GO.` → `A TRAVELER ASLEEP AT MECCA.` → `HIS FEET POINT AT THE KAABA.`

segments.voice: The qazi wakes him roughly. How dare you point your feet at the house of God? And Nanak, tradition says, answers without any anger at all. Then please, turn my feet toward the direction where God is not. Bhai Gurdas, an early Sikh poet, tells it in his verses, and he includes a wonder: when the qazi dragged Nanak by the feet, Mecca itself turned with them. Whether it's a miracle or a picture, the question is the heart of it. Which way is God not? Here's the thing that makes this story generous rather than rude. The qazi's own tradition already agrees with the answer. Muslims face the Kaaba to pray as one community, in one direction; they don't say God lives inside a building. The Qur'an itself says that the east and the west both belong to God, and that wherever you turn, there is the face of God. So the story isn't a Sikh scoring a point off Islam. Sikhs tell it as Nanak reminding a pious man of something his own faith already held, the way a friend might remind you of your own best idea. And for Sikhs it echoes the very first symbol of their scripture. If there is one, and the one is in everything, then there is no direction to point your feet that's empty of God. Not east, not west, not down. Every direction is full.
screen: `TURN MY FEET WHERE GOD IS NOT.` · `BHAI GURDAS TELLS IT IN HIS VERSES.` · `WHEREVER YOU TURN, THE FACE OF GOD.` · `EVERY DIRECTION IS FULL.` · then, large: `WHICH WAY IS GOD NOT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: face four directions, slowly. Stand up if you can. Face one way, take a breath, and just notice what's in front of you, even if it's a wall. Then turn a quarter, and breathe again. Then another quarter. Then the last. If you believe in God, you can ask with each turn: is God here too? If you don't, notice that every direction has something in it worth seeing. The bell holds the time.
Feet toward the Kaaba. Guru Nanak at Mecca, asked to turn his feet away from God's house, asking which way God is not. Today's word.
Your line: which way is god not. Today, in the least holy-looking place you visit, the parking lot, the laundry room, ask it once. Day thirty-seven.

38.title: The hand on the rock
38.hook: tradition says that at Hasan Abdal a boulder rolled down at him stopped at his open palm
38.howItsDone: Sikh pilgrims visit Gurdwara Panja Sahib at Hasan Abdal, in Pakistan, where they touch the handprint in the stone and bathe in the spring.

segments.voice: Yesterday, feet toward the Kaaba, and a calm question in Mecca. Your line was which way is god not. Where did you ask it? Day thirty-eight.

It's a hot day in the hills of what's now northern Pakistan, near a town called Hasan Abdal. Two travelers have been walking a long time, and one of them, Mardana, is desperately thirsty. There's no water below. But at the top of the hill, tradition says, lives a holy man named Wali Qandhari, and he has a spring. So Mardana climbs up and asks for a drink. And he's turned away. He climbs down, and Nanak sends him back up to ask again. Turned away again. A third time. Nothing. A cup of water is about the smallest thing one traveler can ask of another, and three times the answer is no. Today, what happened at the bottom of that hill.
screen: `A HOT DAY NEAR HASAN ABDAL.` → `MARDANA ASKS FOR WATER, THREE TIMES.` → `THREE TIMES, TURNED AWAY.`

segments.voice: Nanak, tradition says, told Mardana to lift a stone at the foot of the hill. Water came up from underneath, clear and cold. And at the top, Wali Qandhari's spring began to fail. Furious, he pushed a huge boulder down the hillside toward the two men. Nanak didn't run. He raised one hand, palm open, and the rock stopped against it. When it settled, the story says, the shape of his hand was pressed into the stone. That handprint is the reason for the name of the place. Panja means the palm of the hand, and the gurdwara there, Panja Sahib, keeps a stone with a handprint that pilgrims still touch, with water running beneath it. Sikh pilgrims still cross the border to visit it. How should we hold a story like this? Like the milk and blood, Sikhs read it in more than one way. Some hold it as a miracle. Others read it as a picture of something every life needs: a hand that stays steady when something heavy comes rolling at you. It's worth saying, too, that the story comes from later tradition, not the scripture, and that people remember Wali Qandhari differently: a shrine to him still stands on that hilltop. So the rock is the center of the story, not the man who pushed it. Notice what Nanak's hand does. It doesn't push back. It doesn't strike. It just holds its ground, open. A steady hand isn't a fist.
screen: `WATER RISES AT THE FOOT OF THE HILL.` · `A BOULDER ROLLS; AN OPEN PALM.` · `PANJA SAHIB — THE PLACE OF THE PALM.` · `NOT A FIST: AN OPEN, STEADY HAND.` · then, large: `A STEADY HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put your palm on a wall, steady. Stand close to a wall, or a door, or a tree if you're outside. Press your palm flat against it. Not hard. Just enough to feel it press back. Breathe, and let your arm be strong without being tense. Think of one heavy thing rolling toward you this week, and let your hand stay open. The bell holds the time.
The hand on the rock. Tradition's story of Guru Nanak's open palm stopping a boulder at Hasan Abdal, the place now called Panja Sahib. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: a steady hand. Today, when something comes at you, a hard email, a sharp word, try an open hand instead of a fist. Day thirty-eight.

39.title: The yogis on the mountain
39.hook: Himalayan yogis ask why he stays in the world; he answers that you live in it without being stained
39.howItsDone: Sikhs follow the householder's path Guru Nanak taught, working and raising families rather than renouncing the world; the Sidh Gosht, his dialogue with the yogis, is part of the Guru Granth Sahib and is studied and sung.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hand on the rock at Hasan Abdal. Your line was a steady hand. When something came at you, did your hand stay open? Day thirty-nine.

On a bad day, the cabin fantasy goes like this. Quit everything. Move to a cabin in the mountains. No inbox, no traffic, no difficult relatives, just silence and snow. In Nanak's time, some people really did it. High in the Himalayas lived the sidhs, yogis who had left the world behind for caves and peaks, and who were said to have mastered the body and the mind. On his journey north, tradition says, Nanak climbed up to meet them. And they were curious about him. Here was a man clearly on a spiritual path, singing about God, and yet he had a wife, children, a home in the plains, and he kept going back to it. Today, the question they asked.
screen: `THE CABIN-IN-THE-MOUNTAINS FANTASY.` → `YOGIS WHO REALLY LEFT.` → `A VISITOR WITH A FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Sidh means one who has succeeded, someone who has reached the goal, a perfected one. These yogis wore earrings and ash and carried begging bowls, and they believed that to find the truth you had to leave ordinary life. Bhai Gurdas tells a version of the meeting in his verses. The yogis ask Nanak how things are going down in the world. And he answers, sharply, that the world is in darkness, because the people who should be lighting it have gone off to hide in the mountains. There's also a long conversation between Nanak and the yogis in the scripture itself, called the Sidh Gosht, the talk with the sidhs, in raga Ramkali. They ask him question after question, and one answer is the heart of this day. How do you live in the world? Like a lotus, he says, which grows in the water but floats clean on top of it. Like a duck, which swims in the stream and comes out dry. You don't have to leave the water. You just don't let it soak in. That's the Sikh ideal in one picture, and it goes right back to Nanak. Not the monk, not the hermit, but the householder: someone who works, raises a family, pays the bills, and keeps God in mind the whole time, unstained by greed and ego. Sikhs don't look down on the yogis' devotion; Nanak spoke with them at length. But his answer was a different path. Stay. Work. Love your people. And float.
screen: `SIDH — ONE WHO HAS SUCCEEDED.` · `WHO LIGHTS THE WORLD, IF YOU HIDE?` · `LIKE A LOTUS, LIKE A DUCK.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH.` · then, large: `IN THE WORLD, UNSTAINED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one ordinary chore with care. The dishes, folding laundry, wiping a counter. For now, settle and choose it, and if you can, begin it while the bell runs. Do it slowly. Feel the water, the cloth, the weight of the plate. Let your mind stay with your hands. This is the lotus: right in the middle of ordinary life, and clean. The bell holds the time.
Sidh. A perfected one, the name for the yogis Nanak met in the mountains, who asked why he stayed in the world. Today's word.
Your line: in the world, unstained. Today, in the busiest moment, picture the lotus on the water, and float for one breath. Day thirty-nine.

40.title: Babur comes
40.hook: Nanak sees the cruelty of Babur's invasion at Saidpur and sings a lament that names the suffering (Asa, ang 360)
40.howItsDone: The Babarvani hymns are part of the Guru Granth Sahib and are sung in kirtan; Sikhs point to them as an example of the Guru speaking out against cruelty and injustice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sidhs on the mountain, and the lotus that floats clean. Your line was in the world, unstained. Which chore did you do with care? Day forty.

Most of the travel stories so far have had a twinkle in them. Water thrown west. Feet pointed at Mecca. A boulder stopped by a palm. Today's story has no twinkle. Remember Saidpur, the town where Lalo the carpenter shared his bread? In the 1520s an army came over the mountains from Kabul, led by Babur, the man who would go on to found the Mughal empire. Saidpur resisted, and it was sacked. Tradition says Nanak and Mardana were there, and were taken prisoner with the townspeople. Most of us know what it's like to see terrible news and scroll past it, because it's too much. Today, what Nanak did instead.
screen: `NO TWINKLE IN THIS ONE.` → `SAIDPUR, THE 1520S.` → `BABUR'S ARMY COMES.`

segments.voice: He sang about it. A small group of Guru Nanak's hymns, which Sikhs call the Babarvani, Babur's hymns, describe the invasion from the inside, and they are some of the most painful verses in the scripture. One of them, in raga Asa, begins with Babur's army sweeping down from Khurasan and terrifying Hindustan. Then the Guru does something startling. He turns to God and asks, in effect: so much suffering, such cries of pain, and did you feel nothing? Another hymn describes the women of the town, whose hair had been braided and adorned with vermilion, now with their heads shaved and dust in their mouths. The palaces are empty. The proud are led away in chains. This is what it means that he did not look away. He names who suffered, and how. He doesn't soften it. He doesn't turn it into a lesson about how the victims deserved it. And he argues with God about it, out loud, in a hymn that has been sung ever since. Sikhs hear several things in these verses. Grief, first. A witness, second: a record of what happened to ordinary people. And a faith that is strong enough to protest, to ask God hard questions without letting go of God. The hymns also say that the rulers of the day had forgotten their duty, and that cruelty comes back on those who do it. With this, the travel stories close. The road that began with Mardana's music ends here, in the ruins of Lalo's town. Tomorrow, Nanak goes home and picks up a plow.
screen: `THE BABARVANI — BABUR'S HYMNS.` · `DID YOU FEEL NOTHING?` · `HE NAMES WHO SUFFERED, AND HOW.` · `A FAITH STRONG ENOUGH TO PROTEST.` · then, large: `HE DID NOT LOOK AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one suffering you've looked away from. Settle, and breathe. It might be far away, a war on the news. It might be close, a neighbor, a relative, someone at work. Don't try to fix it in two minutes. Just name it, and let yourself look at it, honestly, for as long as the bell runs. If you pray, you can hold it before God, even with a hard question. The bell holds the time.
Babur comes. The invasion of Saidpur, and the hymns in which Guru Nanak named the suffering and questioned God. Today's word.
Your line: he did not look away. Today, when hard news appears, read one story all the way through before you scroll on. Day forty.

41.title: The farmer at Kartarpur
41.hook: after the travels he settles by the Ravi, farms the land, and the first Sikh community gathers around him
41.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Kartarpur, now in Pakistan, as the place where Guru Nanak lived out the pattern of work, worship and sharing that gurdwaras follow today; the Kartarpur Corridor has let pilgrims from India visit Gurdwara Darbar Sahib there when it is open.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Babur comes, and the hymns that named the suffering at Saidpur. Your line was he did not look away. Did you read one hard story all the way through? Day forty-one.

You'd expect the ending to go differently. A man walks for years. He's argued with priests, sung for kings and robbers, met yogis in the snow, been taken prisoner by an army. By now people far beyond his village know his songs. So where does a man like that end up? In a palace? A great temple? A cave on a mountain? None of those. He goes to the banks of the river Ravi, in the Punjab, takes off his traveler's clothes, and picks up a plow. Today, the town where the Guru became a farmer.
screen: `YEARS ON THE ROAD.` → `NOT A PALACE. NOT A CAVE.` → `A PLOW, BY THE RAVI.`

segments.voice: The town was called Kartarpur. Kartar means the Creator, and pur means town, so Kartarpur is the Creator's town. Tradition says Nanak founded it himself, and he lived there for the rest of his life. And what he did there is the whole point. He farmed. He worked his own fields. His wife and sons lived with him. And a community gathered around him: farmers, traders, people of every caste, Hindus and Muslims. Bhai Gurdas, the Sikh poet, describes the rhythm of the place. In the early morning, before work, the hymns: the Japji, the long hymn that opens the scripture. In the evening, more singing. In between, a day's honest labor. And a common kitchen, where everyone ate together. Look at what that adds up to. Every idea from the travels, turned into an ordinary Tuesday. Kirat, honest work, like Lalo the carpenter. Sharing, in the kitchen. Remembering God, morning and evening. In the world, unstained, like the lotus. Nanak didn't just tell the yogis to live in the world. He came home and showed them how. That's why Sikhs often speak of Kartarpur as the first Sikh community, a pattern gurdwaras still echo. And the place is still there. Kartarpur is now in Pakistan, just across the border from India, and for a long time Sikhs in India could only look at it from the border. In recent years a corridor opened so Indian pilgrims could cross and visit, though it has been closed at times since.
screen: `KARTARPUR — THE CREATOR'S TOWN.` · `HE WORKED HIS OWN FIELDS.` · `HYMNS AT DAWN, WORK, HYMNS AT DUSK.` · `THE FIRST SIKH COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `HE CAME HOME AND FARMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: work with your hands for five minutes. Settle first, and decide what. Water a plant. Knead dough. Repot something. Scrub a pan. Fix a hinge. Start now if you can, and let the bell run while you work. Feel the weight of it, the texture. No phone, no podcast. Just the work, the way a farmer at Kartarpur might have done it between a morning hymn and an evening one. The bell holds the time.
Kartarpur. The Creator's town, by the river Ravi, where Guru Nanak farmed and the first Sikh community gathered. Today's word.
Your line: he came home and farmed. Today, take one big idea you care about and give it an ordinary job, at home. Day forty-one.

42.title: The tests of Lehna
42.hook: tradition says a disciple named Lehna carried a bundle of wet grass and did every task the Guru asked without complaint
42.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the tests of Lehna as a teaching on seva, selfless service, and on setting aside ego; the story is often told to explain why Guru Nanak chose Lehna, not his sons, as his successor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kartarpur, the Creator's town, where the Guru took up a plow. Your line was he came home and farmed. What big idea did you give an ordinary job? Day forty-two, the end of a week.

Somewhere near you there's a task nobody wants. The overflowing trash. The spreadsheet from 2014. The phone call to the angry customer. Sometimes one person just quietly does it. One day at Kartarpur, a man arrives in fine clothes. His name is Lehna. He's a trader from a nearby town, and tradition says that for years he led a band of pilgrims to a goddess temple in the hills. But on one journey, tradition says, he heard someone reciting Guru Nanak's hymn, the Japji, and he couldn't get it out of his head. So he came to meet the man who wrote it. He found an old farmer in the fields. Today, what happened next.
screen: `THE TASK NOBODY WANTS.` → `A TRADER IN FINE CLOTHES.` → `HE HEARD THE JAPJI, AND CAME.`

segments.voice: Nanak was coming in from the fields with bundles of grass cut for the cattle, soaking wet and dripping mud. Lehna offered to carry one. It ruined his fine clothes. Tradition says the Guru's wife worried aloud about the stains, and Nanak answered that those weren't mud stains; they were saffron, the color of honor. The stories go on like that. The Guru asks for a muddy ditch to be cleared in the middle of the night; Lehna does it. A bowl falls into dirty water; Lehna climbs in after it. The Guru's own sons, tradition says, found reasons to refuse these tasks. Lehna didn't argue, didn't sulk, didn't point out how overqualified he was. He just did each thing, and did it well. How should we hear this? Sikhs don't tell it as a story about a man who did whatever he was told. They tell it as a story about ego: the part of us that says, this is beneath me. Lehna had been a leader with a following of his own. At Kartarpur he became a servant of servants, and that's exactly why he was trusted. And look back at the week. Water thrown west at Hardwar. Feet toward the Kaaba. A steady hand on the rock. The yogis on the mountain. Babur, and a Guru who did not look away. Kartarpur and the plow. And now Lehna and the wet grass. The travels asked big questions. Kartarpur answered them with small, daily work, and in Lehna, the Guru found someone who understood.
screen: `WET GRASS ON FINE CLOTHES.` · `NOT MUD: SAFFRON.` · `THE DITCH, THE BOWL, THE NIGHT.` · `THE TEST WAS EGO.` · then, large: `JUST DO IT WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one task without a word of complaint. Settle, and pick it now: the one you've been putting off because it's boring, or dirty, or beneath you. Picture yourself doing it. If a little voice starts to grumble, don't argue with it; just let it talk while your hands work. Then, today, do the task, and do it well. The bell holds the time.
The tests of Lehna. Wet grass, a muddy ditch, a fallen bowl, and a disciple who did each task well, without complaint. Today's word.
Your line: just do it well. Today, take the task nobody wants, and finish it before anyone asks. Day forty-two.

fork.setup: you arrive in fine clothes to meet a famous teacher. he's carrying a dripping bundle of wet grass. what do you do?
options: wait until he's cleaned up.
offer to carry it, clothes and all.

fork.reveal: Lehna carried it himself. when the mud stained his clothes, tradition says Nanak called the stains saffron, the color of honor.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Lehna, the name he had before he became the second Guru; tradition plays on lehna, what is owed, or due.

trapdoor: what you thought: a disciple who did chores.
what it means: a leader who became a servant, and a test not of obedience but of ego.
what a scholar hears: the tests come from later tradition, not the scripture, and are told to explain why Nanak passed over his sons for Lehna.
